questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the five places a new cloud deployment usually breaks?
options: Network/routing, security group/NSG rules, DNS resolution, IAM/RBAC permissions, and resource quotas/limits
CPU speed, disk brand, cable length, monitor resolution, and keyboard layout
Only the security group — every other layer is reliable by default
Database schema design, front-end styling, color contrast, font choice, and image compression
questions.explain: These five layers are the ones that overwhelmingly turn out to be the real cause behind a vague "it's broken" ticket.

questions.q: In Lesson 31, meridian-web2 couldn't be reached by SSH. Which of the five places was the actual root cause?
options: Network/routing — the instance launched into the wrong subnet with no public IP
DNS resolution — the hostname pointed at the wrong record
A resource quota being hit on the account
An IAM policy missing the SSH permission
questions.explain: The instance was placed in the private subnet by mistake, which meant no public IP and no route to the internet gateway — a routing/placement problem, not a firewall or identity one.

questions.q: In Lesson 32, a new VM's SSH connection hung. Which of the five places was the actual root cause?
options: Security group/NSG rules — a rule still pointed at an old, stale office IP range
A DNS record that had never been created
A missing RBAC role on the admin's account
The VM's operating system had crashed on boot
questions.explain: The NSG rule itself was never wrong when written — it just no longer matched the office's new public IP after a move, which silently dropped the traffic.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an IAM/RBAC permission gap can be tricky to diagnose?
options: Because it looks exactly like a broken resource until you actually read the error text
Because IAM and RBAC never actually cause real outages
Because permission errors always report as a DNS failure
Because every cloud provider disables IAM by default
questions.explain: A permission gap can produce the same kind of vague "it doesn't work" symptom as a network or DNS problem, so the error message itself is what points you in the right direction.

questions.q: Why does a resource quota or limit being hit sometimes produce no obvious configuration error?
options: Because the deployment or scaling action simply fails against a provider-enforced ceiling that isn't a setting you configured wrong
Because quotas are always disabled on production accounts
Because quota limits only apply to storage, never to compute
Because hitting a quota always triggers an automatic quota increase
questions.explain: Quotas like vCPU count, IP limits, or API rate limits exist to protect shared infrastructure, and hitting one can block an action even though nothing in your own configuration is actually wrong.
